frame.what_would_confirm: LSASS memory access or dumping (e.g., procdump, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, Mimikatz), SAM/SECURITY hive or NTDS.dit extraction, suspicious access to credential stores, or use of stolen credentials from those hosts.

T1003.name: OS Credential Dumping
T1003.reason: Credential dumping activity confirmed via LSASS full-access handles from PowerShell/wsmprovhost under user pbeesly on scranton and nashua, inside a broader intrusion (Invoke-Exfil, PsExec64 with cleartext password, WebDAV staging).

T1003.001.name: LSASS Memory
T1003.001.reason: PowerShell.exe (scranton, 03:05:16Z) and wsmprovhost.exe (nashua, 03:09:29Z) opened LSASS with 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff, corroborated by Security 4656/4663 with SubjectUserName pbeesly.

T1003.002.name: Security Account Manager
T1003.002.reason: SAM_SERVER handles with 0xf003f and SamSs registry handles on scranton during the intrusion window, but requested by lsass.exe itself (SCRANTON$); no hive export or SAM file creation seen.

T1003.003.name: NTDS
T1003.003.reason: No ntds/.dit file creation, no vssadmin/shadow/procdump command lines, no directory replication access on the DC.

T1003.004.name: LSA Secrets
T1003.004.reason: No SECURITY\Policy\Secrets access; registry hits limited to HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 and benign CredentialEnrollmentManager/CredentialGuard keys.

T1003.005.name: Cached Domain Credentials
T1003.005.reason: Only routine HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes; no process read the cached-credential store.

T1003.006.name: DCSync
T1003.006.reason: No drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync strings in process command lines or PowerShell script blocks; DC PowerShell blocks are DSC/AD module content.

T1040.name: Network Sniffing
T1040.reason: The only packet-capture activity (netsh.exe trace start capture=yes writing an .etl to C:\windows\TEMP on scranton.dmevals.local, 03:19:17 UTC) was spawned by and stopped by the Microsoft Azure Network Watcher agent (NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service), alongside its logman GAEvents/RTEvents ETL tracing and Test/Install/Start service lifecycle. No pktmon/windump/tcpdump/rawcap/dumpcap/Wireshark command lines, no capture driver image loads, and no PowerShell capture scripting were observed; the 7045 service installs (javamtsup.exe, PSEXESVC.exe) are unrelated to sniffing. Zeek window does not overlap and shows no capture-specific activity.

T1056.name: Input Capture
T1056.reason: Suspicious .scr (scranton) and C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe (nashua) payloads opened 0x1FFFFF handles to conhost/cmd/powershell, consistent with input capture/injection, but no capture mechanism was directly observed.

T1056.001.name: Keylogging
T1056.001.reason: No keyboard-hook registry keys, keylogger services, or GetAsyncKeyState/keylog/SetWindowsHookEx script blocks; registry writes were routine service/system configuration.

T1056.002.name: GUI Input Capture
T1056.002.reason: No credential-prompt spoofing or GUI input capture artifacts in the retrieved events.

T1056.003.name: Web Portal Capture
T1056.003.reason: Zero hits for wwwroot/inetpub/aspx writes, IIS/appcmd/w3wp command lines, or login/auth/signin HTTP URLs.

T1056.004.name: Credential API Hooking
T1056.004.reason: DMEVALS\pbeesly PowerShell (scranton) and wsmprovhost (nashua) requested 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff handles to lsass.exe including read/write process memory — credential API hooking/memory access pattern.

T1110.name: Brute Force
T1110.reason: Zero 4625 failed logons, zero 4771/4776 failures and zero 4740 lockouts in windows.security; the only 4776 is a success (Status 0x0). No brute-force authentication pattern exists.

T1110.001.name: Password Guessing
T1110.001.reason: event.code:4625 count is 0 across all four hosts for the entire window; no repeated failed authentication against any account.

T1110.002.name: Password Cracking
T1110.002.reason: No cracking tools or hash output files were found, but PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, pbeesly) opened lsass with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff on scranton and wsmprovhost.exe opened lsass with 0x1f3fff on nashua — dump-grade access that produces crackable material. The SAM_SERVER 4656 events are lsass itself during a restart (benign).

T1110.003.name: Password Spraying
T1110.003.reason: No spray (no failures), but PsExec64.exe on scranton reused the cleartext pbeesly password against \\NASHUA, producing matching 4648 events and PSEXESVC.exe-spawned python.exe on nashua — single-credential reuse rather than spraying.

T1110.004.name: Credential Stuffing
T1110.004.reason: No failed logons and only one account (pbeesly) used with explicit credentials; no evidence of a stolen credential list being replayed across hosts.

T1111.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
T1111.reason: No MFA/smart-card provider interception was observed (smart-card registry writes were Windows baseline by smss.exe/taskhostw.exe/services.exe). However, on scranton.dmevals.local a hidden steganographic PowerShell loader (PID 2976, parent control.exe, user pbeesly) ran Get-PrivateKeys to export cert:\LocalMachine private keys to C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx (created 03:04:57, deleted 03:08:51) and opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff; wsmprovhost.exe on nashua also opened lsass with 0x1f3fff. This is theft of authentication certificate material that can defeat MFA, so the technique family is present as credential/MFA-material theft rather than interception.

T1187.name: Forced Authentication
T1187.reason: No forced-authentication artefacts: LSASS 4663 events are 0x10 reads by CollectGuestLogs.exe/MsMpEng.exe/machine accounts; the only StartUp shortcut (hostui.lnk) targets a local path as part of a local persistence chain; SMB 445 connections go only to internal 10.0.0.4/10.0.1.6 and a link-local IPv6 address; no WebDAV/NTLM/Responder script blocks (C104 zero hits).

T1212.name: Exploitation for Credential Access
T1212.reason: Full-access LSASS handles (0x1fffff/0x1f3fff) were taken by PowerShell on scranton and wsmprovhost on nashua inside a pbeesly intrusion (Sysinternals toolkit, sdelete, PsExec with cleartext password, hidden encoded PowerShell), but no evidence of exploiting a vulnerable service/application to gain them: no exploited-process child spawns, no Mimikatz/sekurlsa script blocks, call traces point to PowerShell/.NET. Credential access is real; the T1212 exploitation vector is unconfirmed.

T1539.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
T1539.reason: No process other than MicrosoftEdge.exe itself touched browser cookie/profile stores; no Sysmon 10 access to browser images, no security 4663 access to Cookies/Login Data/Web Data, and no PowerShell script block referencing cookie databases. The C112 hits were substring false positives ('DataStore', lastalive*.dat). Malicious activity present in the window (screen capture/keystroke script, WebDAV exfil, sdelete, PsExec python.exe) does not involve web session cookie theft.

T1552.name: Unsecured Credentials
T1552.reason: Hardcoded plaintext credentials ("saribas", "lolol", "MyCozyPassw0rd!") in attacker PowerShell tooling on scranton.dmevals.local, plus recursive *pass*/*login* file sweep and cert export.

T1552.001.name: Credentials In Files
T1552.001.reason: PowerShell on scranton recursively collected user-profile files matching *psw*/*pass*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn* into $env:APPDATA\Draft.Zip, then staged Downloads for WebDAV exfiltration.

T1552.002.name: Credentials in Registry
T1552.002.reason: All 24 credential/Winlogon registry value sets came from services.exe, svchost.exe, winlogon.exe, lsass.exe and wininit.exe; no reg query/save/export or SAM/SECURITY object access.

T1552.003.name: Shell History
T1552.003.reason: No ConsoleHost_history, history.txt or Get-Content activity in PowerShell, Sysmon process/file or 4663 events.

T1552.004.name: Private Keys
T1552.004.reason: Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates with Export-PfxCertificate to C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx on scranton.dmevals.local.

T1552.006.name: Group Policy Preferences
T1552.006.reason: SYSVOL 5145 reads are gpt.ini/GptTmpl.inf policy refresh by machine accounts; no Groups.xml, cpassword or gpprefdecrypt activity.

T1555.name: Credentials from Password Stores
T1555.reason: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) running as pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local opened LSASS with 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF (Sysmon 10) and Security 4656 shows AccessMask 0x1F3FFF including 'Read from process memory', inside a malicious .scr -> cmd -> powershell intrusion chain.

T1555.003.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
T1555.003.reason: No access to Chrome Login Data/Local State or Firefox logins.json/key4.db in file-creation, process-creation or object-access events; only an unrelated svchost INetCookies write.

T1555.004.name: Windows Credential Manager
T1555.004.reason: No vaultcmd/cmdkey/Credential Manager activity and no vaultsvc access; LSASS handle access is attributed to T1555, other LSASS accessors are system/AV processes.

T1555.005.name: Password Managers
T1555.005.reason: No KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass process, file or script activity on any host.

T1556.name: Modify Authentication Process
T1556.reason: Real credential-access activity is present (hidden steganographic PowerShell on scranton opening lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF, and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua with 0x1F3FFF), but no authentication-process modification was observed — no LSA/SecurityProviders/NetworkProvider registry changes, no third-party module loaded into lsass, no 4657/4739/5136 hits.

T1556.001.name: Domain Controller Authentication
T1556.001.reason: 4624/4648 logons are routine machine-account and pbeesly activity (including PSEXESVC lateral movement); no DC authentication tampering, no LSA registry modification, no 4739/5136.

T1556.002.name: Password Filter DLL
T1556.002.reason: No 4657 or 4104 activity referencing Notification Packages, PasswordFilter or lsa keys; the 36 registry-value modifications were certificate and WMI Autologger writes.

T1556.005.name: Reversible Encryption
T1556.005.reason: Zero 4739 events and no Reversible/Set-ADAccountControl/Set-ADUser/dsmod references in 4688, 4103, sysmon or windows.other.

T1556.006.name: Multi-Factor Authentication
T1556.006.reason: No 4739 domain-policy-change events and no MFA-related configuration activity in any retrieved event.

T1556.007.name: Hybrid Identity
T1556.007.reason: Zero 5136 directory-service object modification events; AD PowerShell seen was generic Get-ADUser/New-ADUser helper code.

T1556.008.name: Network Provider DLL
T1556.008.reason: No sysmon registry-set or file-create on NetworkProvider paths and no 4657 NetworkProvider modification; matching registry hits were benign notification/AppContainer writes.

T1557.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
T1557.reason: An on-path condition is proven at L2 (duplicate MAC for 10.0.1.4) and the spoofed path carries SMB/RPC/WinRM toward 10.0.1.6, but no Windows-side AiTM artifact (no DNS client registry tampering, no relayed auth) was found; the Windows hits themselves (4670 token DACLs, 4697/7045 service installs, PsExec) are benign or belong to other techniques.

T1557.001.name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
T1557.001.reason: SMB 445 / RPC 135 / WinRM 5985 sessions to 10.0.1.6 are carried by the spoofed MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1, and NetBIOS name-service broadcasts are on the wire, but no successful relay or poisoned resolution is directly evidenced (SMB sessions are RSTO).

T1557.002.name: ARP Cache Poisoning
T1557.002.reason: MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 claims source IP 10.0.1.4 from 00:33:26Z onward in parallel with the legitimate MAC 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, interleaved on the same destinations/ports — classic ARP cache poisoning by an on-path attacker.

T1557.003.name: DHCP Spoofing
T1557.003.reason: No DHCP traffic at all: no UDP 67/68 in Zeek conn or Sysmon network events, no DHCP server events (1341/1342/1020/1063 zero hits), no dhcp/rogue strings in PowerShell logs.

T1558.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
T1558.reason: Hidden steganographic PowerShell (PID 2976, user pbeesly) on scranton opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff, and wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff — full LSASS access enabling Kerberos ticket/key extraction.

T1558.001.name: Golden Ticket
T1558.001.reason: All 4768 krbtgt TGTs are pre-authenticated (PreAuthType 2) AES256 requests with Status 0x0; no forged-TGT indicators or krbtgt/mimikatz strings.

T1558.002.name: Silver Ticket
T1558.002.reason: 4769 service tickets are all AES256 (0x12), Status 0x0, for legitimate machine accounts; no forged service-ticket evidence.

T1558.003.name: Kerberoasting
T1558.003.reason: No RC4 (0x17) TGS requests, no SPN enumeration or Kerberoast/Rubeus tooling in any dataset.

T1558.004.name: AS-REP Roasting
T1558.004.reason: All AS requests require pre-authentication (PreAuthType 2); no asreproast/GetNPUsers/DontReqPreAuth activity.

T1606.name: Forge Web Credentials
T1606.reason: No forged web credential material. 4624 logon processes are Kerberos/Advapi dominated with only benign User32/NtLmSsp/'-' entries; the sole token-keyword PowerShell hit is the Sysinternals Get-AttributesMask helper; rare process-access masks are normal system-process interactions.

T1606.001.name: Web Cookies
T1606.001.reason: The six rundll32 davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 invocations are spawned by svchost -k LocalService -s WebClient as the OS WebDAV redirector storing cookies for the attacker's own WebDAV share used by Invoke-Exfil; no browser cookie theft or forged cookie injection seen.

T1606.002.name: SAML Tokens
T1606.002.reason: No ADFS/SAML tooling, token-signing certificate artifacts or SAML-derived logons. The only certificate activity is Get-PrivateKeys exporting LocalMachine certs to coyn5igj.3io.pfx (local cert theft), and 4648 logons are PsExec-based, not forged SAML assertions.

T1621.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Request Generation
T1621.reason: 5 planned checks, all with zero hits

T1649.name: Steal or Forge Authentication Certificates
T1649.reason: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell (user pbeesly) ran Get-PrivateKeys, which recursively enumerated cert:\LocalMachine and used Export-PfxCertificate with hardcoded password 'saribas' to write private-key-bearing .pfx files into Downloads (Sysmon file-create for C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 03:04:57Z by powershell.exe PID 3876). The certificates were then compressed into C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\OfficeSupplies.7z, copied to WebDAV \\192.168.0.4\webdav, and the .pfx/.bmp/.png/archive were deleted by Invoke-BeachCleanup (Sysmon event 23 at 03:08:51Z). The lone 4657 SystemCertificates ROOT modification on nashua.dmevals.local was made by C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe under SYSTEM and is benign certificate-store maintenance.

findings.title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access masks by PowerShell and wsmprovhost under user pbeesly
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, running as pbeesly) opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff — PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS-class rights used for memory dumping, with a short UNKNOWN-module call trace. The same activity repeated on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z from C:\windows\system32\wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, PowerShell remoting host, user pbeesly) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff, call trace through System.ni.dll / Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll. Windows Security corroborates: 4656 handle requests to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe with AccessMask 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff by powershell.exe on scranton (SubjectUserName pbeesly) and by wsmprovhost.exe on nashua (SubjectUserName pbeesly), followed by 4663 read (0x10) events. This is not the baseline pattern: the dominant LSASS accessor is svchost.exe with 0x1000 (293 of 326 events), and the only other high-mask accessors are Defender MsMpEng.exe and Azure CollectGuestLogs.exe. The pbeesly session on scranton is independently malicious (Invoke-Exfil script, PsExec64 to \\NASHUA with cleartext password, davclnt.dll WebDAV staging to 192.168.0.4, hidden encoded PowerShell), so the LSASS full-access handles are credential dumping in the course of that intrusion.

findings.title: pbeesly PowerShell/wsmprovhost requests full-access (0x1F3FFF / 0x1FFFFF) handles to lsass.exe on scranton and nashua
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16Z (23:05:16 -04:00) the account DMEVALS\pbeesly, running as C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe (PID 0xba0, logon 0x372E81), requested two handles to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe on scranton.dmevals.local with AccessMask 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff — including 'Read from process memory', 'Write to process memory', 'Perform virtual memory operation' and 'Duplicate handle into or out of process'. At 03:09:29Z the same account requested a 0x1f3fff handle to lsass.exe on nashua.dmevals.local from C:\Windows\System32\wsmprovhost.exe (PID 0x1e28, logon 0x85AAD2), i.e. over a PowerShell remoting session. These are the only non-system, non-AV LSASS handle requests in the dataset (the other 4656 lsass hits are CollectGuestLogs.exe, MsMpEng.exe and lsass.exe itself under machine accounts). Full-access process handles to LSASS from PowerShell are the classic credential-API-hooking / memory-read pattern used to extract logon credentials. No 4104 script block containing lsass/minidump/sekurlsa/hook strings was found, so the exact tooling is not visible in PowerShell logging.

findings.title: PowerShell steganography loader on scranton exported certificate private keys (PFX) and opened LSASS with full access
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell (PID 2976, parent control.exe) that decoded a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEX'd it. The session then ran discovery, persistence steps, accesschk, and a Get-PrivateKeys function that enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports each certificate with a private key to a random .pfx in the user's Downloads folder (password 'saribas'). At 03:04:57 a file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx was created by powershell.exe and at 03:08:51 the same file was deleted (Sysmon 23) by powershell.exe. At 03:05:16 the same PowerShell process (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (full access) with an UNKNOWN call trace, i.e. direct credential-store access from the attacker's PowerShell. This is credential material theft (certificate private keys usable for authentication / MFA-bypass via certificate-based logon) rather than interception of an MFA provider; no smart-card/MFA provider tampering was observed. Related: on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (WinRM PowerShell) opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29, and pbeesly credentials were used explicitly via PSEXESVC.exe (4648, target localhost) at 23:11:40 local, consistent with reuse of the stolen account.

findings.title: Unsecured credentials: hardcoded plaintext passwords in attacker PowerShell tooling on SCRANTON
findings.summary: Across scranton.dmevals.local the pbeesly PowerShell session (2020-05-01 22:56–23:08) contains multiple hardcoded plaintext secrets in script blocks: "saribas" used as the .pfx export password in Get-PrivateKeys, "lolol" as the 7-Zip archive password in Invoke-Exfil, and "MyCozyPassw0rd!" for the cozy account used to mount \\192.168.0.4\webdav. Combined with the recursive *pass*/*login* file sweep and the certificate export, this is credential collection and staging on a compromised host, followed by SMB/PsExec reuse of pbeesly against nashua.dmevals.local.

findings.title: Recursive user-profile sweep for password/login-named files archived to Draft.Zip on SCRANTON
findings.summary: At 2020-05-01T22:56:17-04:00 on scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly's PowerShell session (PID 5944) ran a script block that recursively enumerates $env:USERPROFILE for documents plus wildcard patterns *psw*, *pass*, *login*, *admin*, *sifr*, *sifer*, *vpn and archives the results with Compress-Archive into $env:APPDATA\Draft.Zip — a classic search of user files for stored credentials. findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exports every LocalMachine certificate to .pfx on SCRANTON
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran a PowerShell script block (ScriptBlock ID 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, Path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) at 2020-05-01T23:04:56-04:00 that defines Get-PrivateKeys: it builds a SecureString from the hardcoded plaintext password "saribas", enumerates cert:\LocalMachine recursively and calls Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint into $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx. One second later Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe. This is private-key/certificate theft staged for exfiltration (the same host then ran Invoke-Exfil compressing Downloads and copying it to a WebDAV share).

findings.title: PowerShell on SCRANTON opened LSASS with full-access mask (0x1F3FFF / 0x1FFFFF) including read-process-memory, in the middle of a hands-on-keyboard intrusion
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local the user pbeesly ran an interactive PowerShell session that was spawned by a malicious screen-saver (C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr -> cmd.exe -> powershell.exe). At 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z that PowerShell process (PID 2976 / 0xba0) opened handles to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF (Sysmon event 10, call trace ending in UNKNOWN module), and Security 4656 recorded the same handle request with AccessMask 0x1F3FFF listing 'Read from process memory' / 'Perform virtual memory operation'. This is the access pattern of an in-memory credential dump of the LSASS password store. The surrounding session shows the same actor staging SysinternalsSuite, running accesschk, Get-PrivateKeys (exporting certs to .pfx), persistence and screen capture, so the LSASS access is attacker credential theft, not a benign tool.

findings.title: Steganographic PowerShell loader on scranton opened LSASS with full-access mask (0x1FFFFF) — credential access, not auth-process modification
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z, control.exe spawned a hidden, execution-policy-bypass PowerShell (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, High integrity) that decoded a payload from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png via System.Drawing GetPixel and IEX'd it. At 03:05:16Z that same process (SourceProcessGUID {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF — full read/write access consistent with in-memory credential dumping. A second full-access LSASS handle came from wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and a .NET/PowerShell call trace. However, no evidence of authentication-process tampering was found: no 4657 registry changes to LSA/SecurityProviders/Notification Packages/NetworkProvider keys, no 4739, no 5136, no 4657 on NetworkProvider, no lsass image-load of a non-Microsoft module (only lsass.exe loading itself at 03:19:09Z), and no 4688/4104 referencing lsass, procdump, comsvcs, MiniDump or mimikatz. The 289 svchost.exe LSASS accesses (0x1000) and the AntimalwareConfig.exe / WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe accesses (0x1400) are routine. Assessment: credential theft activity is real, but the T1556 family itself is not observed.

In the Zeek window (2020-04-30 00:06–00:45Z) host 10.0.1.4 normally sources traffic from MAC 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2 (134 conn records, 00:06:38–00:45:00). Starting 00:33:26.283Z a second, different MAC fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1 also appears as zeek.orig_l2_addr for the same source IP 10.0.1.4 (44 conn records through 00:45:00.042Z), interleaved with the legitimate MAC on the same destinations and ports (e.g. 10.0.1.6:5985 at 00:33:26, 10.0.1.6:445 at 00:35:25, 10.0.1.6:55121 from 00:36:17). Two distinct L2 addresses claiming one IP simultaneously is the signature of ARP cache poisoning / an on-path attacker, not of a normal NIC change (which would replace, not interleave with, the original MAC). The attacker MAC's traffic is directed at the peer host 10.0.1.6 (NASHUA) on SMB 445, RPC 135, WinRM 5985, HTTP 80 and high port 55121, consistent with interception of that host's traffic.

findings.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported all LocalMachine certificates to password-protected .pfx files on SCRANTON, then staged and exfiltrated them
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, in the context of user pbeesly (S-1-5-21-1830255721-3727074217-2423397540-1107), a PowerShell script block named Get-PrivateKeys (script block 9d153741-75c3-4062-afe3-aeca0aee611b, loaded from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1) enumerated the entire cert:\LocalMachine store recursively and called Export-PfxCertificate for every certificate with a thumbprint, writing each to $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads\<random>.pfx protected by the hardcoded password 'saribas'. At 03:04:57.460Z Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe (PID 3876) — the same PID that hosted the Get-PrivateKeys script block. findings.title: SAM_SERVER handle with 0xF003F requested by lsass.exe on scranton during the intrusion
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, Security 4656 events show handles requested to ObjectName 'SAM' (Object Server 'Security Account Manager', Object Type SAM_SERVER) with AccessMask 0xf003f (DELETE, READ_CONTROL, WRITE_DAC, WRITE_OWNER, ConnectToServer, ShutdownServer, InitializeServer, CreateDomain, EnumerateDomains, LookupDomain) at 03:19:21-03:19:22Z and 03:20:46Z, plus handles to \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Services\SamSs at 03:19:10Z. The requesting process is C:\Windows\System32\lsass.exe under SubjectUserName SCRANTON$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3e7), i.e. the SAM service itself, which is the normal owner of these objects — no non-lsass process was seen reading the SAM hive. No reg save / hive export command lines were found (only dsregcmd.exe and sc.exe start pushtoinstall registration matched the reg/save/SAM/ntds pattern), and no SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive files were created on disk (only Prefetch .pf files matched). The timing inside the pbeesly intrusion window keeps this worth noting, but the actor and access path are the legitimate SAM server, so I cannot attribute SAM dumping.

findings.title: Suspicious .scr and python.exe payloads on scranton/nashua open full-access (0x1FFFFF) handles to conhost/cmd/powershell
findings.summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr (PID 8524, launched by explorer.exe as DMEVALS\pbeesly at 02:55:56Z, SHA256 0DF38A55D940F498478EB03683C94D4584236E100125B526A67650BA54DF4AE4) opened 0x1FFFFF handles to conhost.exe and cmd.exe at 02:56:04Z and 02:57:12Z; the file was later wiped with sdelete64.exe at 03:02:04Z. On nashua.dmevals.local, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe (PID 2172, spawned by another C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe, user DMEVALS\pbeesly) opened 0x1FFFFF handles to powershell.exe (03:15:48Z) and cmd.exe (03:16:40Z). Full-access handles to console/shell processes are consistent with input capture / process injection, but no keyboard-hook, GetAsyncKeyState or keylogger registry artifacts were observed, so the capture mechanism itself is not proven.

findings.title: No offline cracking tooling or hash-dump artifacts; lsass access by PowerShell/wsmprovhost is credential dumping, not cracking
findings.summary: No hashcat/john/cracking binaries appear in the 447 process-create events, and no .pot/.hash/ntds.dit output files appear among 1649 file-create events. However, the lsass process-access stack shows two non-system processes opening lsass with dump-grade access: PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, spawned by control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter with a hidden -ep bypass IEX-from-bitmap loader) opened lsass with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff then 0x1fffff on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z, and wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, user pbeesly, PowerShell remoting) opened lsass with 0x1f3fff on nashua.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:09:29Z. Security 4656/4663 corroborate the same handles (0x1f3fff/0x1fffff on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe). The 10 SAM_SERVER 4656 events are all lsass.exe itself under SCRANTON$ at 23:19-23:20 local, coinciding with a system restart (wininit/csrss re-opening lsass at 03:19:09Z), i.e. benign. The 0x1fffff/0x1f3fff lsass handles are the credential-theft step that would feed offline cracking, but no cracking itself was observed.

findings.title: No password spraying; the only explicit-credential logons are PsExec reuse of the already-known pbeesly password
findings.summary: There are no 4625 failures, so no spray pattern exists. The 15 4648 explicit-credential events are: 9 for pbeesly (5 on scranton.dmevals.local targeting NASHUA from 10.0.1.6, 4 on nashua.dmevals.local from C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe), plus DWM-1/DWM-2/UMFD-0/UMFD-1/UMFD-2/SCRANTON$ from winlogon/wininit/taskhostw (normal session setup). The pbeesly 4648s pair with PsExec64.exe being run on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:11:18Z with the cleartext password on the command line (\\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe), followed by python.exe launching on nashua.dmevals.local under PSEXESVC.exe at 03:11:40Z. This is reuse of a single already-obtained credential for lateral movement, not spraying across many accounts.

On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice within 31 ms at 2020-05-02T03:05:16 (GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff, call trace ending in UNKNOWN modules), and on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29. These are the only high-access LSASS handles in the window; the other 317 LSASS accesses are svchost/Azure agent reads at 0x1000/0x1400. The surrounding activity on scranton is hands-on-keyboard by user pbeesly: accesschk.exe (03:04:34), sdelete64.exe against Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip (03:03:14/03:03:33), csc.exe/cvtres.exe compiling from C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Local\Temp (03:08:03), PsExec64.exe to \\NASHUA with the cleartext password for dmevals\pbeesly (03:11:18), and hidden encoded PowerShell plus 'Get-ItemPropertyValue HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Javasoft ... | Invoke-Expression' spawned from hostui.exe (03:21:27). However, nothing retrieved shows exploitation of a vulnerable service/application to obtain these handles: no crash-then-child pattern, no service/app process spawning children (parents are services.exe, svchost.exe, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, Azure agents), no Mimikatz/sekurlsa script blocks (4104 search returned none), and the LSASS call traces point to PowerShell/.NET rather than an exploited process. Credential access is real but the T1212 exploitation vector is unconfirmed.
findings.title: LSASS accessed with full-access rights by PowerShell (scranton) and wsmprovhost (nashua) during a pbeesly intrusion — no exploitation of a vulnerable service observed

findings.summary: The poisoned L2 path is used for SMB (445), RPC endpoint mapper (135), WinRM (5985) and HTTP (80) sessions toward 10.0.1.6, i.e. the attacker MAC is positioned on the SMB/RPC path where NTLM relay would occur. Zeek also records NetBIOS name-service broadcasts to 10.0.1.255:137 from 10.0.1.4 (00:35:01.874Z) and from 10.0.1.6 (00:34:51.731Z) — the name-resolution traffic that is poisonable for SMB relay. However, no relayed authentication or poisoned name resolution is directly proven: the SMB sessions to 10.0.0.4 are RSTO (reset/timeout) and the 4624 records show only normal machine-account (type 3) and pbeesly logons. The Windows-side DNS client registry keys (Sysmon 13 *DNSClient*) had zero hits, so no host-level name-resolution tampering is visible.
findings.title: SMB/RPC/WinRM traffic to NASHUA (10.0.1.6) carried by the spoofed MAC; NetBIOS name-service broadcasts on the wire
No NTDS.dit access or copy observed
findings.summary: No evidence of NTDS.dit theft. File-creation events matching ntds/.dit/.dmp returned only two Windows Error Reporting crash dumps (C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\WER\Temp\WER51F5.tmp.dmp and WER5437.tmp.dmp), and no process command line contained ntds, vssadmin, shadow or procdump. The domain controller newyork.dmevals.local shows only machine-account network logons (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, WEC$, SCRANTON$ type 3) and no directory-service replication access was observed.

findings.title: LSA secrets not accessed by any non-system process
findings.summary: The only LSASS accessors with elevated rights were the malicious PowerShell/wsmprovhost handles (covered under T1003.001); all other LSASS handle sources are baseline (svchost.exe 289 events at 0x1000, Azure AntimalwareConfig.exe 15, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 13, plus wininit/csrss/services). Registry modifications touching SECURITY/LSA paths were limited to HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 (5 events) and benign CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc / CredentialGuard service keys; no SECURITY\Policy\Secrets access was observed.

findings.title: Cached domain credential store (SECURITY\Cache) not read by attacker tooling
findings.summary: Registry writes to HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 (5 events) are the only cached-credential-related modifications and are consistent with normal logon cache maintenance; the remaining 'Cache' matches are unrelated (NetworkList NLA cache, TaskCache, AppContainer Internet Settings cache). No process was observed reading the SECURITY\Cache hive, and the LSASS access that could expose DCC2 hashes is the same PowerShell/wsmprovhost activity already reported under T1003.001.

findings.title: No DCSync / DRSUAPI replication abuse observed
findings.summary: No process command line or PowerShell script block contained drsuapi, lsadump, dcsync or Invoke-Mimikatz. The only PowerShell script blocks on the DC newyork.dmevals.local are DSC resource modules (xDNSServerAddress, xStorage, MSFT_ScriptResourceStrings) and AD cmdlet help text, all running as SYSTEM. Directory replication access was not observed on newyork.dmevals.local.

findings.title: netsh trace packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local is Azure Network Watcher agent telemetry, not adversary sniffing
findings.summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:19:17 UTC the only packet-capture activity in the whole dataset appeared on scranton.dmevals.local: netsh.exe was launched as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (LogonId 0x3E7) with 'netsh.exe trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"'. Both Sysmon EID 1 and Security EID 4688 show the parent as C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe (PID 3180, '/service'), and the capture was stopped 7 seconds later by the same parent ('netsh.exe trace stop'). The surrounding activity is the Azure guest-agent/Network Watcher lifecycle: NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service at 03:19:13, logman.exe stop/create/start of GAEvents and RTEvents writing to C:\WindowsAzure\Logs\*.etl, and NetworkWatcherAgent.exe Test/Install/Start /service /autoStart at 03:20:41-42. No third-party or offensive capture tooling was found: no pktmon, windump, tcpdump, rawcap, dumpcap, Wireshark or promiscuous-mode command lines in Sysmon EID 1 or Security 4688, no capture-related driver/image loads (pktmon/npcap/wpcap/ndiscap) in Sysmon EID 6, and no PowerShell capture scripting (4104 check C047 zero hits). The 7045 service installs in windows.other are javamtsup.exe and repeated PSEXESVC.exe (pbeesly) on nashua, unrelated to packet capture. Zeek data (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows window and shows only ordinary conn/ssl/dns/smb/kerberos logs with no capture-specific record type. Conclusion: T1040 is not evidenced as attacker behaviour; the netsh trace is legitimate Azure platform network diagnostics.

findings.title: No keylogger artifacts: no keyboard-hook registry writes or keylogging script blocks
findings.summary: The 17,541 Sysmon registry-value-set (event 13) events are dominated by W32Time, DeliveryOptimization, UserAssist, BAM and ContentDeliveryManager keys; the 1,357 hits for Keyboard/keylog/Services registry paths are ordinary service configuration writes (e.g. svchost.exe writing HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\W32Time\Config\LastKnownGoodTime). No 4104 script block contained GetAsyncKeyState, keylog or SetWindowsHookEx. No keylogger persistence or configuration key was observed.

findings.title: No GUI input capture (credential prompt spoofing) observed
findings.summary: No evidence of fake credential dialogs or GUI input capture was found in the retrieved data; the only GUI-adjacent activity is the .scr payload's full-access handles to conhost/cmd, which is reported under T1056 rather than as GUI prompt capture.

findings.title: No web portal capture: no IIS/wwwroot/aspx writes or login-page HTTP activity
findings.summary: Checks for file writes to wwwroot/inetpub/.aspx, IIS/appcmd/w3wp command lines, PowerShell referencing wwwroot/inetpub/appcmd, and HTTP URLs containing login/auth/signin all returned zero hits, so no web portal credential-capture activity was observed.

findings.title: No brute-force authentication activity observed; credential theft was done by dumping lsass, not by guessing
findings.summary: Across the whole windows.security window (2020-05-02T02:55:25Z..03:28:09Z, 4 hosts) there are zero 4625 failed-logon events, zero 4771/4776 failure statuses and zero 4740 lockouts. The only 4776 in the dataset is a successful NTLM validation (Status 0x0) for pbeesly on newyork.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:20:40-04:00. Successful 4624 logons are dominated by machine accounts (NEWYORK$ 123, SCRANTON$ 37, NASHUA$ 25) and pbeesly (20, type 3), consistent with normal service/network logons. No authentication-failure burst exists to support a brute-force hypothesis.

findings.title: No password guessing: zero 4625 events on any host
findings.summary: The count of event.code:4625 in windows.security is 0 for the entire collection window, so there is no repeated failed authentication against any account or host that would indicate password guessing. The credential access that did occur on scranton.dmevals.local was memory-based (lsass handle with 0x1fffff), not password guessing.

findings.title: No credential stuffing: no failed logons and no multi-account credential list use
findings.summary: Credential stuffing requires many failed authentications from a list of stolen credentials; windows.security contains 0 events with event.code:4625 and no 4771/4776 failure statuses, and the 218 type-3 network logons involve only machine accounts plus pbeesly. The single account used with explicit credentials is pbeesly, so there is no evidence of stuffing a credential list against the hosts.

findings.title: Smart-card / crypto registry and service activity is Windows baseline, not MFA interception
findings.summary: The only smart-card/crypto-related registry writes were made by core Windows processes during normal boot/startup on scranton.dmevals.local: smss.exe setting Cryptography\Calais symbolic links, taskhostw.exe writing CertificateTemplateCache timestamps, and services.exe writing an MUICache entry for SCardSvr.dll ('Smart Card'). No smart-card or MFA provider DLL was registered, replaced or configured by a non-system process, and no script block referenced smart-card/MFA APIs (the three 4104 hits were unrelated module/help text and an exfiltration function). The 7045 service installs were javamtsup.exe and repeated PSEXESVC.exe (PsExec lateral movement by pbeesly), not MFA-provider tampering. LSASS handle opens with 0x1000/0x1400 by svchost.exe, AntimalwareConfig.exe and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe are routine security/telemetry reads.

findings.title: No forced-authentication (T1187) activity observed; LSASS reads and SMB traffic are benign system/administrative behaviour
findings.summary: Hunting for T1187 on 2020-05-02 02:55–03:28Z found no coercion artefacts. The six 4663 events on lsass.exe objects are all AccessMask 0x10 (read) by machine accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$, UTICA$) via C:\WindowsAzure\Packages\CollectGuestLogs.exe and MsMpEng.exe, plus one by pbeesly via powershell.exe — routine Azure guest-agent/AV/administrative reads, not credential dumping or forced auth. The three shortcut files created (Sysmon 11) are Explorer 'Recent' .lnk files for pbeesly and a StartUp\hostui.lnk written by powershell.exe on scranton.dmevals.local; the hostui.lnk is part of a local persistence chain (hostui.txt dropped from SysinternalsSuite, Invoke-Persistence -PersistStep 1/2, then hostui.bat -> powershell Start-Process C:\Windows\System32\hostui.exe -verb runas) and points to a local path, not a UNC/WebDAV resource, so it does not force outbound NTLM. SMB (Sysmon 3, port 445) traffic goes only to internal addresses 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6 and a link-local IPv6 address, and 5145 IPC$ access shows pbeesly using samr/svcctl/PSEXESVC against newyork and nashua from 10.0.1.4 — lateral PsExec-style administration, not authentication coercion to an attacker host. No WebDAV/NTLM/Responder script blocks were found (C104 zero hits).

findings.title: No web session cookie theft observed; browser cookie-store activity on scranton is MicrosoftEdge.exe's own profile I/O
findings.summary: Hunting for T1539 across windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell and windows.other (2020-05-02 02:55–03:28Z) found no evidence of cookie-store theft. The only events touching browser cookie/profile paths are on scranton.dmevals.local under user pbeesly, and every one of them is performed by MicrosoftEdge.exe itself: Sysmon 23 file-delete of Edge AC\Temp ~DF*.TMP files at 03:18:33, Sysmon 11 creation of ...\MicrosoftEdge\User\Default\DataStore\_TempTestAccess.txt at 03:21:05, and Sysmon 11 creation of Edge RecoveryStore .dat and further ~DF*.TMP files at 03:21:05–03:21:06. A query for any non-Edge process touching *microsoftedge*, *google*, *mozilla* or *cookies* paths returned only svchost.exe creating C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\...\AC\INetCookies and Prefetch GOOGLEUPDATE.EXE-B95715F5.pf entries — normal OS/updater behaviour. No Sysmon 10 process-access to chrome/firefox/msedge/iexplore images (check C114, zero hits), no security 4663 object access to Cookies/Login Data/Web Data/Edge/Chrome/Mozilla paths, and no PowerShell 4104 script block referencing cookies, Login Data, sqlite or browser profile paths. The C112 'Cookies/Login Data/Web Data' aggregate hits were false positives from the substring 'DataStore' in GroupPolicy and Edge paths plus lastalive*.dat, not browser credential stores. Separately, the same window does contain clearly malicious activity on scranton.dmevals.local by pbeesly (Invoke-ScreenCapture/Keystroke-Check script block, Invoke-Exfil staging to \\192.168.0.4\webdav, sdelete64 wiping C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr) and PsExec-delivered C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local, but none of that activity reads or exfiltrates browser cookie databases, so it is not T1539.

findings.title: Registry credential-key writes are OS components only — no adversary registry credential access
findings.summary: The 24 Sysmon registry value-set events touching Password/Credential/Winlogon paths are all attributable to Windows components: services.exe (10), svchost.exe (6), winlogon.exe (6), lsass.exe (1) and wininit.exe (1) on scranton/nashua, covering keys such as CredentialGuard\Enabled, CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc_13619b and Winlogon\PasswordExpiryNotification. No reg query/save/export command lines and no 4663 access to SAM/SECURITY/Password objects were found, so no registry credential harvesting is evidenced.

findings.title: SYSVOL/GPO reads are routine machine-account policy refresh, not GPP cpassword harvesting
findings.summary: The 38 5145 SMB accesses to \\*\SYSVOL are gpt.ini, Policies, Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf reads performed by computer accounts (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$, NASHUA$) from their own IPs during normal Group Policy refresh; no Groups.xml, cpassword, gpprefdecrypt or AES-key script/command activity was found in PowerShell, Sysmon process or file events.

findings.title: No browser credential-store access observed
findings.summary: Hunting for browser password stores (Chrome 'Login Data'/'Local State', Firefox logins.json/key4.db) found no file creation, no process command line and no object-access audit referencing them on any host. The only file-creation hit was an unrelated INetCookies file written by svchost.exe under the LocalService service profile on scranton.dmevals.local, which is normal Windows behaviour. The actor on scranton did run a recursive file-collection script matching *pass*, *login*, *admin* patterns and compressed the results, but no browser credential database was touched in the retrieved events.

findings.title: No Windows Credential Manager (vault/cmdkey) harvesting observed; LSASS access is covered under T1555
findings.summary: No vaultcmd, cmdkey or Credential-Manager command lines appeared in Sysmon process creation or Security 4688, and no process-access events targeted vaultsvc. The only 'vault/credential' text hits were benign: a Credential Guard configuration message (event 14) on scranton.dmevals.local and PowerShell script blocks containing unrelated words ('validate', 'Get-CommonADParameters'). The rare LSASS handle masks (0x1F3FFF/0x1FFFFF by PowerShell.exe as pbeesly on scranton) are reported under T1555; the remaining LSASS accessors (svchost.exe with 0x1000/0x101001 via lsm.dll, wininit.exe/csrss.exe at boot, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe and AntimalwareConfig.exe with 0x1400) are normal system/AV behaviour.

findings.title: No password-manager (KeePass/1Password/Bitwarden/LastPass) access observed
findings.summary: No process creation, process access, file creation (.kdbx/keepass/1password/bitwarden), Security 4688 or PowerShell script block referencing a third-party password manager was found on any of the four hosts. The only credential-adjacent theft in the data is the LSASS handle access on scranton.dmevals.local, which is not a password-manager store.

findings.title: No domain-controller authentication tampering; 4624/4648 logons are routine machine-account and pbeesly activity
findings.summary: 297 successful logons (4624) are dominated by machine accounts NEWYORK$ (123), SYSTEM (60), SCRANTON$ (37), NASHUA$ (25) and the user pbeesly (30); the 218 network logons (LogonType 3) are loopback/IPv6 machine-account authentications on newyork.dmevals.local. The 15 explicit-credential logons (4648) are pbeesly re-using its own credentials, including four from C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe on nashua.dmevals.local between 23:11:40 and 23:15:03 local time — consistent with lateral movement by the same actor, not with a backdoor authentication mechanism. No 4657 changes to LSA/SecurityProviders keys, no 4739 policy changes, no 5136 directory-service changes, and no lsass image-load of a third-party module were observed, so no DC authentication-process modification is evidenced.

findings.title: No password-filter (Notification Packages) DLL registration observed
findings.summary: No 4657 registry-value modification referenced Notification Packages, lsa or Password keys, and no PowerShell 4104 script block mentioned Notification Packages, PasswordFilter or HKLM\...\lsa. The 36 registry-value modifications (4657) that do exist are unrelated: certificate blob writes by C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe on nashua.dmevals.local and WMI Autologger EventLog-Application value changes by wevtutil.exe on scranton.dmevals.local. No password-filter DLL was registered.

findings.title: No reversible-encryption or account-control changes; no 4739 policy events
findings.summary: Event 4739 (domain policy change) returned zero hits, and no 4688 command line, PowerShell 4103 payload, sysmon process creation or windows.other message referenced Reversible, Set-ADAccountControl, Set-ADUser or dsmod. The only AD-related PowerShell script blocks seen were generic Get-ADUser/New-ADUser helper functions on newyork.dmevals.local, not account-flag changes. No reversible-encryption tampering is evidenced.

findings.title: No MFA modification observed
findings.summary: No 4739 domain-policy-change events were returned in windows.security, and nothing in the retrieved events touched multi-factor authentication configuration. The observed malicious activity (steganographic PowerShell loader, LSASS handle with 0x1FFFFF, WebDAV exfiltration to 192.168.0.4) does not include MFA tampering.

findings.title: No hybrid-identity / directory-service object modification (5136) observed
findings.summary: Event 5136 (directory service object modified) returned zero hits in windows.security, so no AD object or hybrid-identity configuration was altered in this window. The AD-related PowerShell on newyork.dmevals.local was read/parameter-helper code, not a federation or sync configuration change.

findings.title: No Network Provider DLL registration observed
findings.summary: No sysmon registry-set (event 13) or file-create (event 11) touched a NetworkProvider path, and no 4657 modification referenced NetworkProvider. The 442 registry-set hits matching lsa/NetworkProvider/Notification/WDigest/SecurityProviders were all benign Windows notification and AppContainer/ContentDeliveryManager writes by Explorer.EXE, RuntimeBroker.exe, DllHost.exe, backgroundTaskHost.exe and SearchProtocolHost.exe. No credential-provider DLL was installed.

The 143 event.code 4670 hits are all 'Object Server: Security / Object Type: Token' permission changes by SYSTEM machine accounts (SCRANTON$, NEWYORK$) from SearchIndexer.exe, svchost.exe and services.exe — routine token DACL churn, not network interception. The 4697/7045 service installs are the Java VM support service (javamtsup) on scranton and repeated PSEXESVC installs on nashua by pbeesly, plus a burst of svchost-based per-user services on scranton. The PsExec64.exe execution on scranton at 2020-05-02T03:11:18Z (parent powershell.exe, user pbeesly) with the command line containing a cleartext password for dmevals\pbeesly and launching C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on \\NASHUA is lateral movement / credential misuse, not adversary-in-the-middle, and is out of scope for T1557. No Windows event in this window shows ARP, DHCP or name-resolution tampering.
findings.title: Windows-side hits (4670 token permission changes, 4697 service installs, PsExec to NASHUA) are benign/adjacent, not AiTM

findings.summary: No DHCP activity exists in any dataset. Zeek conn logs contain no UDP 67/68 flows (UDP destination ports are only 53, 389, 138, 123, 137). Sysmon event.code 3 UDP destinations likewise show no 67/68. windows.other contains no DHCP-server events (1341/1342/1020/1063 returned zero hits) and windows.powershell has no dhcp/rogue references. The only broadcast traffic is normal NetBIOS name service (137/138) and NTP/DNS. Nothing indicates a rogue DHCP server or DHCP option tampering.
findings.title: No DHCP spoofing observed — no DHCP traffic, no rogue DHCP server events
No golden-ticket indicators: krbtgt TGTs are normal pre-authenticated AS exchanges
findings.summary: All 14 4768 events on newyork.dmevals.local are ordinary AS-REQ/TGT issuance for krbtgt with PreAuthType 2 (pre-authentication performed), TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256) and Status 0x0, for accounts pbeesly and the machine account SCRANTON$. No forged-TGT hallmarks (RC4 0x17, missing pre-auth, anomalous lifetimes) appear, and no krbtgt/golden/mimikatz strings exist in PowerShell or other Windows logs. The LSASS full-access reads above are the precursor to krbtgt theft, but no golden-ticket use is evidenced in this window.

findings.title: No silver-ticket indicators in TGS requests
findings.summary: The 28 4769 events on newyork.dmevals.local are service-ticket requests for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all with Status 0x0 and AES256 (0x12) encryption, issued to pbeesly and SCRANTON$ from 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6. No RC4-encrypted service tickets, no anomalous service names, and no silver/service-ticket strings in any log. Nothing indicates forged service tickets.

findings.title: No Kerberoasting: no RC4 TGS bursts or SPN enumeration
findings.summary: No 4769 request uses RC4 (0x17) encryption, the signature of Kerberoasting, and no SPN/Kerberoast/Rubeus strings appear in PowerShell or other Windows logs. Zeek kerberos data (2020-04-30, non-overlapping window) shows only 14 AS and 11 TGS requests with a single error type KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED, consistent with normal authentication. The observed TGS volume is low and tied to machine-account service access.

findings.title: No AS-REP Roasting indicators
findings.summary: Every 4768 in the dataset carries PreAuthType 2, meaning Kerberos pre-authentication was required and performed; AS-REP Roasting depends on accounts with pre-auth disabled. No asreproast/GetNPUsers/DontReqPreAuth strings were found in Sysmon process command lines, PowerShell script blocks, or other Windows logs.

findings.title: No forged web credentials observed; certificate export and WebDAV cookie activity are unrelated to T1606
findings.summary: Across windows.security, windows.sysmon and windows.powershell (2020-05-02 02:55–03:28Z) there is no evidence of forged web credential material. The 4624 logon-process stack is dominated by Kerberos (217) and Advapi (76) with only 2 User32, 1 NtLmSsp and 1 '-' entries; the User32/NtLmSsp entries are pbeesly interactive (type 10) and network (type 3) logons from 172.18.39.2 on scranton, and the '-' entry is a SYSTEM type-0 boot logon — all normal. The single PowerShell 4104 hit matching token/cookie keywords is the Sysinternals helper function Get-AttributesMask in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\readme.ps1 (SE_GROUP_* token attribute constants), not credential forging. The rare Sysmon process-access masks resolve to svchost/consent/wininit/Explorer/service-host interactions with system processes (e.g. wininit.exe -> lsass.exe 0x1000000, services.exe -> svchost.exe 0x18), which are normal Windows behaviour. Separately, the host does show a real intrusion (pbeesly running discovery, persistence, screen capture, keystroke jobs, sdelete and WebDAV exfiltration to 192.168.0.4), but that is credential/certificate theft and exfiltration, not T1606 web credential forging.

findings.title: WebDAV DavSetCookie invocations are WebClient-service artifacts of the exfiltration script, not forged web cookies
findings.summary: Six rundll32.exe executions of 'davclnt.dll,DavSetCookie 192.168.0.4 http://192.168.0.4/webdav' ran as DMEVALS\pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:08:50 and 03:10:22-23Z (Sysmon 1 and Security 4688). Their parent is svchost.exe -k LocalService -p -s WebClient, i.e. the Windows WebDAV redirector service, and they coincide with the WebClient service start at 03:08:47Z. This is the normal mechanism by which the WebClient service stores WebDAV auth cookies when the PowerShell Invoke-Exfil function maps \\192.168.0.4\webdav via New-PSDrive — the cookie is being set by the OS for the attacker's own WebDAV share, not a forged/stolen web session cookie being injected. No cookie-file writes to browser stores were found; the only cookie-related file creation is a benign INetCookies package path under the LocalService profile. The underlying exfiltration is malicious, but it is not T1606.001.

findings.title: No SAML token forging; certificate export via Get-PrivateKeys is local cert theft, not token-signing abuse
findings.summary: No SAML/ADFS token-signing activity exists in the data: no ADFS service, no SAML tooling, no token-signing certificate registry or file artifacts, and no 4624/4648 logons attributable to forged SAML assertions. The 4648 explicit-credential logons are 9 for pbeesly (PSEXESVC.exe on nashua and pbeesly->NASHUA from 10.0.1.6 on scranton) plus DWM/UMFD/SCRANTON$ machine-account entries — PsExec lateral movement, not SAML. The one certificate-related action is PowerShell function Get-PrivateKeys (readme.ps1) run by pbeesly at 03:04:56Z, which enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports each certificate to a random .pfx in Downloads with password 'saribas'; this produced C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 03:04:57Z. That is local private-key/certificate theft (a Credential Access action) but it is not forging of SAML tokens, so T1606.002 is not observed.

incidents.title: LSASS memory accessed with full-access masks by PowerShell (scranton) and wsmprovhost (nashua) under pbeesly
incidents.rationale: All describe the same LSASS handle events: PowerShell.exe PID 2976 on scranton.dmevals.local opening lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff/0x1fffff at 2020-05-02T03:05:16Z and wsmprovhost.exe PID 7720 on nashua.dmevals.local with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29Z. The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1003.001 (LSASS Memory); the other technique labels (T1056.004, T1110.002, T1212, T1555, T1556, T1558) are alternative interpretations of the same events, and F15/F21 explicitly note no cracking or exploitation was observed.

incidents.title: SAM_SERVER and SamSs registry handles requested by lsass.exe on scranton
incidents.rationale: Security 4656 events show handles to the SAM object (SAM_SERVER, AccessMask 0xf003f) and to the SamSs service registry key requested by lsass.exe on scranton.dmevals.local; this is the SAM credential-dumping technique, assessed suspicious/low confidence.

incidents.title: Hardcoded plaintext passwords in attacker PowerShell tooling on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: Script blocks contain hardcoded plaintext secrets ('saribas', 'lolol', 'MyCozyPassw0rd!') used by the attacker tooling, combined with the credential file sweep and certificate export — unsecured credentials in attacker tooling on a compromised host.

incidents.title: Recursive user-profile sweep for password/login-named files archived to Draft.Zip on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: PowerShell recursively enumerated the user profile for *psw*/*pass*/*login*/*admin*/*vpn files and archived them to Draft.Zip — searching user files for stored credentials (Credentials In Files).

incidents.title: PowerShell Get-PrivateKeys exported LocalMachine certificate private keys to .pfx on SCRANTON
incidents.rationale: All describe the same Get-PrivateKeys script block (from readme.ps1) enumerating cert:\LocalMachine and exporting every certificate with a private key to a password-protected .pfx in pbeesly's Downloads, later staged into OfficeSupplies.7z. The best-fitting in-scope technique is T1552.004 (Private Keys); T1649 is an alternative label for the same action.

incidents.title: SMB/RPC/WinRM traffic carried by spoofed MAC and NetBIOS name-service broadcasts
incidents.rationale: The poisoned L2 path carries SMB/RPC/WinRM toward 10.0.1.6 and NetBIOS name-service broadcasts are on the wire, positioning the attacker for name-resolution poisoning/SMB relay; no relayed authentication is directly proven, so assessed suspicious.

incidents.title: ARP cache poisoning: second MAC impersonating 10.0.1.4
incidents.rationale: A second MAC (fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) appears as orig_l2_addr for source IP 10.0.1.4 interleaved with the legitimate NIC MAC — ARP cache poisoning.

incidents.title: PsExec reuse of known pbeesly credentials to move to NASHUA
incidents.rationale: The 4648 explicit-credential events pair with PsExec64.exe run on scranton.dmevals.local using the cleartext pbeesly password to launch python.exe on NASHUA; no password spraying occurred. This is remote-service lateral movement, not credential access.

incidents.title: Suspicious .scr and python.exe payloads opening full-access handles to conhost/cmd/powershell
incidents.rationale: The observed action is execution of a malicious screen-saver and dropped python.exe payloads that open 0x1FFFFF handles to console/shell processes; this is process execution/injection behavior rather than credential access, so it is out of scope.
